pulls.title: cli: Parse -signetchallenge like bitcoind
pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

```
$ bitcoind -signet -signetchallenge=z
Error: -signetchallenge must be hex, not 'z'
```

The error returned by `bitcoin-cli` only indicates that the RPC cookie wasn't found. It doesn't hint at invalid hex:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -signet -signetchallenge=z getblockcount
error: Authorization failed: ...
Is your -signetchallenge correct for custom signets?
```

To have consistent validation of signet args in `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-cli`, we now parse `-signetchallenge` in a new `ReadSignetChallengeArg()` function which is called in `GetSignetDataDir()` and `ReadSigNetArgs()`.

Addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34566#discussion_r3668123074

I didn't add a release note because I don't think this change of an error message warrants one.

pulls.title: ci: add native freeBSD ci job
pulls.body:
This replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation job with a native build and test job inside a FreeBSD VM. NetBSD and OpenBSD retain their existing cross-compilation jobs.

We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds. This starts with FreeBSD because it has been the most reliable BSD platform in the nightly jobs.

As we don't have native FreeBSD runners, the job uses [vmactions/freebsd-vm](https://github.com/vmactions/freebsd-vm), which is also used by the nightly builds. It reuses the existing CI scripts, depends build, and cache actions where possible.

The VM image is cached after its `prepare` step installs dependencies. The job also restores and saves the usual build caches. Initial testing on free GitHub Actions runners took approximately 60 minutes without caches and 20–30 minutes with caches populated. Performance on Warp runners remains untested.

The VM uses the runner's available CPU count and 75% of its RAM, leaving the remaining memory for the host and VM overhead. There is some overhead after testing while `rsync` copies cache directories back out of the VM.

The patchset also suppresses `lsof` warnings on FreeBSD that would otherwise interfere with functional tests.

The job requires enabling one additional action:

```text
vmactions/freebsd-vm@v1
```

pulls.title: validation: Leave some pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked`, fix another `nSequenceId` issue
pulls.body:
`m_blocks_unlinked` serves two purposes:
 1. finding blocks to `setBlockIndexCandidates` once their parents are
       received
 2. setting `m_chain_tx_count` once the parents are received

In case the parent block of a previously pruned block is received,  2. is currently not being done, because pruning removed the entries from `m_blocks_unlinked`.
This can result in `CheckBlockIndex` failures (#31512, #36021) and incorrect rpc results, plus we are in a temporarily inconsistent state (`m_chain_tx_count` is currently not set, but would get set if we restarted).

This scenario is unlikely to happen during normal node operation unless there are huge reorgs, but it can happen, for example, in `getblockfrompeer` scenarios.
Fix this by leaving pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked` that don't have `m_chain_tx_count` set, and also adding them on restart. 

This was one of two reasons, the fuzz target `block_index_tree` couldn't cover pruning of blocks not in the main chain.

The other one is similar to #34521 and #35070 - if we receive a block a second time (after pruning), we could change `nSequenceId` while the block is in `setBlockIndexCandidates` - fix this by attempting to remove it from the set before re-adding it.

After the two issues are fixed, the restriction from `block_index_tree` fuzz target is removed.

Fixes #36021
Fixes #31512

pulls.title: mining: include chunks that reach block limits
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `BlockAssembler` fills block templates with mempool chunks that fit the configured weight limit and the consensus sigops limit, but currently rejects a chunk when it brings either total exactly to its limit.
Equality is valid because [`block_max_weight` is a maximum](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/b811aeabad94ef48cd0f0fb1d2fcc456594aeedb/src/node/mining_types.h#L59-L65) and [BIP 141 defines both consensus limits using `≤`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0141.mediawiki#other-consensus-critical-limits).
The `>=` checks can therefore leave valid capacity unused and omit a fee-paying chunk.
Mining option validation also permits [`block_max_weight == MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/ed7dd7cf4e1561a97edf72eba29a67b14e28c717/src/node/mining_args.cpp#L43-L46) and [`coinbase_output_max_additional_sigops == MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS_COST`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/ed7dd7cf4e1561a97edf72eba29a67b14e28c717/src/node/mining_args.cpp#L55-L59), while the chunk checks reject an accounted total equal to either limit.
A [2016 review comment on the original package-selection PR](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/7600#discussion_r67020333) raised the same inclusive-limit point.

**Fix:** Use strict greater-than comparisons so exact-limit chunks are included.
Extend the existing chunk-limit test to cover exact fits and one-unit overages for both weight and sigops.
Clarify how mining software reserves weight and sigops for the completed block.

This addresses the first issue in #35596.

pulls.title: net: stop sharing P2P listeners with automatic Tor services
pulls.body:
**Problem:** With a normal `-bind` (but no dedicated onion bind), automatic Tor services can forward incoming connections to the normal P2P listener, where they may be misclassified and inherit IP-based whitelist permissions.

**Fix:** If no dedicated onion bind exists, keep Tor control available for outbound proxy discovery but skip automatic incoming service creation and warn after authentication.
The node starts with its configured listeners (including the default onion listener when no `-bind` is supplied), and Tor control starts only after those listeners have been opened successfully.

Affected nodes need a concrete `-bind=<addr>:<port>=onion` to restore incoming Tor connections.

Wildcard onion binds are rejected at startup when `-listenonion` is enabled, while their classification with `-listenonion=0` remains outside this change.

qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: mining: use steady clock for waitNext timeout
pulls.body:
Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

Use the steady clock for the deadline and tick. `NodeClock` is kept only for the testnet 20-minute rule, which must compare node time with the tip's timestamp.

pulls.title: rpc: Let dumptxoutset fail early on stale targets and concurrent runs
pulls.body:
This improves handling of two edge cases where `dumptxoutset` currently only fails after doing unnecessary and possibly incorrect work:

Stale rollback target (first commit): `ParseHashOrHeight` accepts any known block hash, and the rollback path never checks the target is on the active chain. The full UTXO set is copied and blocks are disconnected back from the tip only to fail when the target block height is reached. This is now rejected before all that as an invalid param, matching the check in `getchaintxstats` and `scanblocks`. This is a pretty unlikely scenario but the fix is also very small.

Concurrent calls (second commit): Nothing prevented triggering two runs at once and since this is a relatively long running operation I don't think it is that unlikely that this might happen by accident or that users think this might actually be a possible thing to do if you want two different dumps. On master currently both runs would write to `<path>.incomplete`, so the second dump to the same path corrupts the file the first one reports as successfully written. And also the prune lock has a fixed name, so the second run overwrites the first's height and the first to finish deletes the others lock mid-rollback. A second call now fails immediately with "dumptxoutset is already running". `TemporaryPruneLock` is extended and renamed to `DumptxoutsetGuard` and handles both the general running of multiple instances and the lock management. The alternative to this approach would be to allow for concurrent runs and fix that behavior but it seemed to me like that would be overengineering considering that the audience for this functionality should be very small.

pulls.title: kernel: Use typed errors for fatal and flush error notifications
pulls.body:
Part of the libbitcoinkernel project (tracking issue #27587 ), specifically the "Remove translation.h usage from the kernel" item. `kernel::Notifications::fatalError()` and `flushError()` take a `bilingual_str`, which pulls `util/translation.h` and the application-level `G_TRANSLATION_FUN` into the kernel library, and translation is an application concern rather than a consensus one. The same interface already shows the way out: `warningSet()` takes a `kernel::Warning` enum, and the node turns it into a translated string in `node/kernel_notifications.cpp`.

Along with removing the dependency, another goal here is separating responsibilities, because the goals of error handling and error reporting are different: presenting an error to a user is an application concern, not something `libbitcoinkernel` itself should own. The error is structured on both sides: in C++ as the full `kernel::FatalError` variant, and in the C API as its numeric value. With the current changes the C side only carries half of that structure today though, the dynamic fields (a block hash, a path, an exception's `what()`) do not cross the C API yet, even though ideally they should.

This PR does the same for the two error notifications. A new `src/kernel/error.h` defines `kernel::FlushError` as a plain enum and `kernel::FatalError` as a `std::variant` with one struct per error, whose fields carry the context the message needs: a block hash, a path, the `what()` of a caught exception, block heights. It holds types and nothing else, so every message is now built on the node side. The exception is `FatalErrorString()` in `validation.cpp`, because a fatal error raised during validation also fails the block through `BlockValidationState::Error()`, which takes the reason as a plain string right there, and `fatalError()` returns void, so the node has no way to put its message into that state. A follow-up could store the typed error in the state instead and let the node create the string message.

This does not remove the kernel's dependency on `util/translation.h`, it is just a step. The other two notifications, `progress()` and `warningSet()`, still take a `bilingual_str`, and `bitcoinkernel.cpp`, `checks.cpp`, `node/chainstate.cpp`, `txmempool.cpp` and `validation.cpp` still include the header.

There is one behavior change to mention here. The two C API callbacks lose their `message` parameter, so they now carry only the error code, the same pattern that `btck_BlockValidationResult` already uses.

pulls.title: validation: don't accept txs to the mempool while loading a snapshot
pulls.body:
`ActivateSnapshot` checks that the mempool is empty before it starts, but `PopulateAndValidateSnapshot` then runs without `cs_main`, which takes minutes on mainnet. A transaction entering the mempool in that window (e.g. through `sendrawtransaction`) hits the assert in `AddChainstate`:

```
Assertion failed: (!prev_chainstate.m_mempool || prev_chainstate.m_mempool->size() == 0), function AddChainstate, file validation.cpp, line 6201.
```

By then the base blockhash file has been written, so the node needs `-reindex` to start again.

This sets a flag on `ChainstateManager` while `ActivateSnapshot` runs, and `AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` reject with `snapshot-loading` while it's set. `testmempoolaccept` still works. A second `loadtxoutset` started while one is running is also rejected.

`test_mempool_blocked_during_load` in `feature_assumeutxo.py` pauses the load through a FIFO, checks that `sendrawtransaction` and `submitpackage` are rejected and the mempool stays empty, then lets the load finish. On master the transaction is accepted and the node aborts. The test is skipped where `os.mkfifo` isn't available.

pulls.title: mining: move getblocktemplate cache into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #35675. This addresses the `getblocktemplate` part of the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35675#pullrequestreview-5299625960.

`getblocktemplate` reuses its last template until the tip changes, or until the mempool changes and the template is more than 5 seconds old. That cache currently lives in four function-local statics, which:

- live as long as the process, so the cached `CBlockIndex*` can outlive its `ChainstateManager` (as in unit tests);
- rely on `cs_main` being held, which nothing checks;
- can't be unit tested.

This PR moves the cache into `BlockTemplateManager`, in three commits:

1. **rpc:** refactors the statics in place into a `CachedBlockTemplate` struct and a `GetNewOrCachedBlockTemplate()` helper, `GUARDED_BY(::cs_main)`. The template's `hashPrevBlock` replaces the cached `CBlockIndex*`, and the 5 seconds becomes `GBT_TEMPLATE_REBUILD_INTERVAL`.
2. **refactor:** moves them into `BlockTemplateManager`. It's easiest to review with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change`.
3. **test:** adds a unit test for each rebuild rule and for the retry after a failed build.

No behavior change is intended, and only `getblocktemplate` uses the cache. It uses `cs_main` rather than its own mutex, since the RPC already holds it and building a template takes it anyway.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

Encrypting existing wallets that are unencrypted is fraught with footguns and complexity both for users and for developers.

For example:

pulls.title: http: support unix sockets
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isolated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

pulls.title: qa: Wait for both alerts in `feature_versionbits_warning.py`
pulls.body:
The node raises the unknown rules warning, and runs the `-alertnotify` command, twice in this test. The first time is when the unknown deployment becomes active, and the second is after the restart. The test checks the alert file only once, at the end. As the command appends to the alert file, that check is already satisfied by the output of the first alert, so the test does not wait for the second command at all.

The first commit waits for the first alert before the restart.

The second commit empties the alert file while the node is down, so that the final check can only be satisfied by the second alert.

On Windows, this narrows a race in which the test directory was removed while the second command was still starting. The command keeps open the handles it inherits from the node, which made the cleanup fail:
```
PermissionError: [WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process:...
```

This PR improves the test logic and mitigates https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28529. However, it does not address the inheritance of the node's handles by child processes, part of which is tracked in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36668.

pulls.title: validation: fix false corruption errors after pruning or AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `getblockfrompeer` restores a pruned block's body without recreating its undo record. If startup verification reaches that block at level >2, it attempts to disconnect it and reports database corruption, preventing the node from restarting.

With ordinary pruning, reaching the restored block requires a deeper check than the default six blocks. The AssumeUTXO case can occur with the default checks.

**Fix:** Stop deep verification when a pruned node reaches missing undo data, using the existing result for unavailable history. The same allowance covers missing undo on AssumeUTXO snapshot chainstates, matching the existing treatment of unavailable snapshot history. Level 4 still reconnects the newer blocks that were disconnected. `verifychain` returns `false` to indicate incomplete verification, including when undo is missing at the snapshot base. Lower verification levels and corruption checks for undo records marked as present retain their existing behavior.

An AssumeUTXO restart can still hit a [separate block-index candidate assertion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36452#issuecomment-6464524112) after verification.

This came up during [pruned `txindex` review](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002). The pending `pruneassumevalid` change also needs verification to handle missing undo correctly, so this fix is being split out to land first.

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
I was researching coin selection when I came across this bug, so I thought I'd fix it

Pr #33223  adjusts  weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes, as confirmed in this [comment ](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36255#discussion_r4432516127)

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

If you reverse #33223, it still passes, which means it misses the tie-break

### The fix
The test now uses `mixed_weight_pool and adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
Lowers the max weight to 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed

This should show failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and pass on master.
